text: You're given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, one digit per node. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — reverse order means the ones digit is at the head. So two, four, three is the number three forty-two, not two forty-three. And that's actually good news. Written addition has to start from the ones digit, because carries travel toward the high end. Here the ones digit is exactly where I start walking. So one pass front to back is already the right order — no reversing, no measuring lengths first. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a hundred nodes each, each digit zero through nine, and no leading zeros except for the number zero itself.

Up to a hundred digits — that's the detail that decides the approach, so let me say it out loud now. These numbers do not fit in any built-in integer type. A long long tops out around nineteen digits, so I'd be short by eighty-one. Quick check on the example: two, four, three plus five, six, four is three forty-two plus four sixty-five, which is eight hundred seven, so the answer is seven, zero, eight. Two things I want to pin down. Can the lists be different lengths? And should I expect the sum to be longer than both inputs, like nine plus one?
Yes to both. Different lengths are allowed, and the sum can be one digit longer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would convert each list to an integer, add them, then split the result back into digits. But it overflows: pack twenty nines into a long long and you get a completely different nineteen-digit number. Another option is to pad the shorter list with zeros first, then add position by position. That's correct, but it costs an extra pass, and I'd still handle the final carry separately. This problem reminds me of grade-school column addition, the same idea big-number libraries are built on. At each position, add the carry and both digits, keep the value mod ten, and pass the tens part forward. The arithmetic never leaves single-digit scale, so input length doesn't matter. I'll build the result with a dummy head, so appending the first node and the tenth are the same line of code.

Here's the plan. One: loop while there's a carry or either list still has nodes. Two: at each position, v is the carry plus whichever digits exist; the new carry is v divided by ten, and v keeps v mod ten. Three: append a new node holding v, and return dummy's next. One thing worth flagging is the loop condition. Carry in there handles nine plus one equals ten, where the sum is longer than either input. And it can't run away: v is at most nineteen, so carry is at most one, and once both lists are empty that last round makes the carry zero. At most one extra round. The two if checks handle unequal lengths on their own — an exhausted list contributes nothing, which is padding with zeros without actually padding. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The line int v equals carry is the whole carry mechanism — it brings the spill-over in before the digits are added; everything else is bookkeeping. One thing worth flagging: there are two allocation decisions here, and they go opposite ways. The new ListNode for each result digit is correct — those nodes are the return value, so they must outlive the call. The dummy never escapes — I return dummy dot next — so it lives on the stack. If I'd written new for the dummy, nothing would ever free it: one leaked node per call. So the useful question isn't should I use new; it's does this thing get handed to the caller?

Let's dry-run the code. Nine, nine, nine plus nine, nine — that's nine ninety-nine plus ninety-nine, expected ten ninety-eight. Round three is the one that matters: l two has run out, so its if simply doesn't fire, and that position adds only the carry and l one — unequal lengths with no special case. Round four exists only because carry is in the loop condition: both lists are empty, and the leftover one becomes the new top digit. The result reads eight, nine, zero, one — ten ninety-eight. That matches. Corner cases: zero plus zero gives a single zero, no stray digit. Nine plus one gives zero, one. One plus nine, nine, nine ripples the carry all the way to zero, zero, zero, one. And a hundred nines plus a hundred nines gives a hundred and one digits.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear in the longer list: every round consumes at least one digit or disposes of the final carry, so the loop runs at most max of m and n, plus one, times. The output is that size too, but the extra space is constant — just carry, v and tail. The worst case is two lists of a hundred nines: a hundred and one digits with a leading one. Oh, one more thing — the ordering. If the digits were stored most significant first, the list walks forward while carries move the other way. I'd use two stacks to pop digits from the ones end and build the result by prepending — no dummy needed. That's linear extra space, and the input stays untouched. So reverse order isn't an odd quirk — it's what keeps this to constant extra space.

Well done. Three things stood out. You ruled out the integer conversion with a number — nineteen digits versus a hundred — instead of vaguely worrying about overflow. You explained the loop condition as one line doing three jobs, and showed why the carry term adds at most one extra round. That's the part people usually patch in after failing a test. And you separated the two allocations by lifetime rather than by habit. Noticing that one escapes and one doesn't is the actual distinction.
